title: Numbers, strings and symbols
goal: Recognize literal values and interpolate a value into a string.
paragraphs: A literal writes a value directly in your program. 7 is an Integer and 7.0 is a Float. Double-quoted strings can insert the result of an expression with #{...}. Single-quoted strings do not perform that interpolation.

A Symbol, such as :ruby, is often used as a name or key. true and false represent boolean values; nil commonly represents an absent value. These are objects too, and you can ask each object for its class.
code:
language = "Ruby"
puts "Hello, #{language}!"
p 7 / 2
p 7.0 / 2
p :ruby.class
p nil.nil?
pitfall: A Symbol and a String with similar spelling are different values: :ruby == "ruby" is false.
remaining: Regular expressions, heredocs, percent literals, numeric bases, Rational and Complex literals need further lessons.

experiments.title: Compare division results
experiments.task: This version divides 7 by a Float. Compare it with Example: what result changes, and why?
experiments.code:
language = "Ruby"
puts "Hello, #{language}!"
p 7 / 2.0
p 7.0 / 2
p :ruby.class
p nil.nil?
experiments.answer: The division result changes from 3 to 3.5. With a Float operand Ruby performs floating-point division; the Example uses two Integers.

experiments.title: Interpolate a value
experiments.task: Change the language value to "Ruby 4". What part of the sentence changes?
experiments.code:
language = "Ruby"
puts "I am learning #{language}."
experiments.answer: Interpolation inserts the current value of language into the double-quoted string.

experiments.title: Compare literal types
experiments.task: Which values have different classes, and are the symbol and string equal?
experiments.code:
p 7.class
p 7.0.class
p :ruby == "ruby"
experiments.answer: 7 is an Integer, 7.0 is a Float, and :ruby is a Symbol distinct from the String "ruby".

title: Assignment and object references
goal: Use local variables and understand when two names refer to the same object.
paragraphs: Assignment associates a name with a value. Reassigning a variable changes what that name refers to. It does not automatically copy an object. This distinction matters when an object can be modified.

Local variable names usually begin with a lowercase letter. Constants begin with an uppercase letter; instance variables begin with @ and will appear in the classes lesson. A method has its own local-variable scope.
code:
name = "Ruby"
other = name
other << "!"
puts name
other = "Python"
puts name
puts other
pitfall: Assignment is not a deep copy. A copy of a collection can still contain references to the same nested objects.
remaining: Multiple assignment, constant lookup, global/class variables and detailed block scope are not covered yet.

experiments.title: Compare shared and copied strings
experiments.task: Compare this run with Example: why does name stay Ruby here, while the Example prints Ruby! first?
experiments.code:
name = "Ruby"
other = name.dup
other << "!"
puts name
other = "Python"
puts name
puts other
experiments.answer: Here name and other start with separate strings because dup copies the string. In Example they refer to the same string, so appending through other changes name too.

experiments.title: Reassign a name
experiments.task: Change the second assignment to "Crystal". What prints?
experiments.code:
language = "Ruby"
language = "Python"
puts language
experiments.answer: A later assignment makes language refer to the new string, so Crystal prints.

experiments.title: Share a mutable string
experiments.task: Why does changing second also change what first prints?
experiments.code:
first = "Ruby"
second = first
second << "!"
puts first
experiments.answer: Both names refer to the same mutable String. Appending through second changes that object.

title: Operators and precedence
goal: Group calculations deliberately and inspect comparisons.
paragraphs: Operator precedence determines how an expression groups its parts. Multiplication groups before addition. Parentheses make a different grouping explicit and can also make your intent easier to read.
== compares values; = performs assignment. Many Ruby operators are method calls on an object, so their behavior depends on the receiver. For example, + adds numbers but joins strings.
pitfall: The words and/or have different precedence from &&/||. Do not mechanically swap them in assignments.
remaining: Operator definitions on custom classes, bitwise operators, safe navigation and boolean assignment precedence need deeper treatment.

experiments.title: Compare the groupings
experiments.task: Compare the second calculation here with Example: why is its result 14 instead of 20?
experiments.code:
p 2 + 3 * 4
p 2 * (3 + 4)
p 5 == 5
puts "Ruby" + " Playground"
experiments.answer: Here 3 + 4 is grouped before multiplying by 2, giving 14. Example groups 2 + 3 first and then multiplies by 4, giving 20.

experiments.title: Compare two expressions
experiments.task: Why do the expressions produce different totals?
experiments.answer: Multiplication groups before addition unless parentheses change the grouping.

experiments.title: Join strings
experiments.task: Change second to " rules". What does + do here?
experiments.code:
first = "Ruby"
second = "!"
puts first + second
experiments.answer: For strings, + joins the receiver and argument into a new string.

title: Choose a branch with if and case
goal: Use conditional expressions and recognize Ruby truthiness.
paragraphs: if selects a branch using a condition. Only false and nil are falsey in Ruby: zero and an empty string are truthy. An if expression also produces the value of its selected branch.

Use elsif to test another condition and else for the fallback. unless runs its branch when a condition is falsey. A case/when expression compares a value against alternatives; ranges can represent groups of numbers.
code:
score = 72
label = if score >= 60
  "pass"
else
  "retry"
end
puts label
puts "zero is truthy" if 0
case score
when 90..100
  puts "excellent"
when 60...90
  puts "on track"
else
  puts "practice"
end
output:
pass
zero is truthy
on track
pitfall: An empty collection is also truthy. Test empty? when you mean “contains no elements”.
remaining: Ternary expressions, modifier parsing details and case equality require further examples.

experiments.title: Compare the selected branches
experiments.task: Compare this run with Example: which case message changes when score is 95?
experiments.code:
score = 95
label = if score >= 60
  "pass"
else
  "retry"
end
puts label
puts "zero is truthy" if 0
case score
when 90..100
  puts "excellent"
when 60...90
  puts "on track"
else
  puts "practice"
end
experiments.answer: The if message stays pass. The case message changes from on track to excellent because 95 matches the first range.

experiments.title: Use an if result
experiments.task: Set temperature to -2. Which branch supplies message?
experiments.code:
temperature = 12
message = if temperature < 0
  "freezing"
else
  "above freezing"
end
puts message
experiments.answer: The condition is true, so the if expression evaluates to "freezing".

experiments.title: Test Ruby truthiness
experiments.task: The supplied code tests nil. Change nil to 0: which branch runs now?
experiments.code:
if nil
  puts "runs"
else
  puts "skips"
end
experiments.answer: The original nil takes the else branch and prints skips. With 0, the first branch prints runs: only nil and false are falsey in Ruby.

title: Repeat work and control a loop
goal: Use iteration, next and break without creating an unbounded loop.
paragraphs: Iteration repeats work for each value. each yields successive values to a block, while while repeats as long as its condition stays truthy. until repeats while its condition is falsey.

next skips the remainder of the current iteration. break leaves the loop. A loop that never changes its condition can run forever; this playground imposes an execution timeout, and its Stop control can cancel a run.
code:
(1..5).each do |number|
  next if number == 2
  break if number == 5
  puts number
end
count = 0
while count < 2
  count += 1
end
p count
pitfall: A .. range includes its end; a ... range excludes it. That can change how many times an iteration runs.
remaining: for-loop scope, redo, retry and loop return values are not covered yet.

experiments.title: Compare loop control
experiments.task: Compare the loop output with Example: why does this run stop after printing 1?
experiments.code:
(1..5).each do |number|
  break if number == 3
  next if number == 2
  puts number
end
count = 0
while count < 2
  count += 1
end
p count
experiments.answer: Here break runs before next when number is 3, so the loop stops before printing 3. Example skips 2, then prints 3 and 4 before reaching its break at 5.

experiments.title: Iterate over a range
experiments.task: Change the range to 1...3. Which number disappears?
experiments.code:
(1..3).each do |number|
  puts number
end
experiments.answer: The exclusive range omits its endpoint, so it prints 1 and 2.

experiments.title: Skip one iteration
experiments.task: What does next do when number is 3?
experiments.code:
(1..4).each do |number|
  next if number == 3
  puts number
end
experiments.answer: It skips the rest of that iteration and continues with 4.

title: Define methods and pass arguments
goal: Define a reusable method with a positional and keyword argument.
paragraphs: A method packages a calculation behind a name. Define it with def and close the body with end. Ruby returns the last evaluated expression unless an explicit return exits the method earlier.

Positional arguments are matched by position. Keyword arguments are passed by name. Defaults let callers omit an argument. Parentheses at the call site make the argument list clear even when Ruby permits omitting them.
code:
def greeting(name, punctuation: "!")
  "Hello, #{name}#{punctuation}"
end
puts greeting("Ruby")
puts greeting("Matz", punctuation: "?")
pitfall: Printing inside a method is different from returning a string. A method ending in puts returns nil.
remaining: Rest arguments, keyword rest, forwarding, destructuring, singleton methods and argument evaluation order need dedicated lessons.

experiments.title: Compare the default argument
experiments.task: Compare the two calls here with Example: which greeting changes, and why?
experiments.code:
def greeting(name, punctuation: ".")
  "Hello, #{name}#{punctuation}"
end
puts greeting("Ruby")
puts greeting("Matz", punctuation: "?")
experiments.answer: The first greeting changes from Hello, Ruby! to Hello, Ruby. because its call uses the default. The Matz call supplies ? explicitly, so it is unchanged.

experiments.title: Return the last expression
experiments.task: Call double with 9. What does the method return?
experiments.code:
def double(number)
  number * 2
end
p double(6)
experiments.answer: The last expression is number * 2, so double(9) returns 18.

experiments.title: Pass a keyword argument
experiments.task: Change the explicit punctuation to "?". What is printed?
experiments.code:
def label(name, punctuation: "!")
  "Hi, #{name}#{punctuation}"
end
puts label("Ruby", punctuation: ".")
experiments.answer: The supplied call prints Hi, Ruby. because it passes a period. After changing that argument to "?", it prints Hi, Ruby?; an explicit keyword overrides the default "!".

title: Yield to blocks and store callable behavior
goal: Pass behavior to a method and call a Proc or lambda.
paragraphs: A block is behavior supplied alongside a method call. A method can invoke it with yield. Block parameters receive the values passed by yield. Blocks can use local variables from their surrounding scope.

A Proc or lambda makes callable behavior available as an object. Invoke it with call. Lambdas enforce argument counts more like methods; Proc and lambda also differ in how return behaves. This example stays with simple expression bodies.

Ruby 3.4 introduced it as an implicit block parameter. In the final expression, it refers to each array element. Use an explicit parameter such as |number| when a descriptive name makes the code easier to follow.
pitfall: Calling yield when no block was supplied raises LocalJumpError. Methods with optional blocks can check block_given?.
remaining: Non-local return, & conversion, block binding precedence and numbered parameters require further lessons.
versionNote: This lesson uses the implicit it block parameter, introduced in Ruby 3.4.

This version uses an explicit block parameter, |number|. The implicit it parameter was introduced in Ruby 3.4 and is not available in this version. Keep the parameter declaration when running this example.

experiments.title: Trace the yielded value
experiments.task: Compare the first result here with Example. Which input changed, and why do the other results stay the same?
experiments.answer: The method yields 5 here instead of 2, so the block result changes from 6 to 15. The Proc and lambda still receive 4, so their results stay 8 and 12.

experiments.title: Yield a value
experiments.task: Change the yielded value to "Matz". What does the block return?

def announce

end
puts announce { |name| "Hello, #{name}" }

puts shout.call("ruby")
experiments.answer: The lambda runs its block body with the argument and returns BLOCKS.

title: Create objects with classes
goal: Initialize instance state and expose behavior through methods.
paragraphs: A class defines behavior for its instances. new creates an instance and calls initialize. Instance variables belong to an object, so separate instances can hold different values.

attr_reader defines a reader method. Public methods form the callable interface; private methods support its implementation. Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and specialize behavior, and super invokes the corresponding superclass implementation.
code:
class Counter
  attr_reader :value
  def initialize(start = 0)
    @value = start
  end
  def increment
    @value += 1
  end
end
first = Counter.new
second = Counter.new(10)
first.increment
p first.value
p second.value
pitfall: attr_reader exposes reading only. It does not generate a value= writer.
remaining: Inheritance examples, super, singleton classes, private/protected methods and constant lookup need further lessons.

experiments.title: Compare instance values
experiments.task: Compare this run with Example: why is first.value 3 here, while second.value stays 10?
experiments.code:
class Counter
  attr_reader :value
  def initialize(start = 0)
    @value = start
  end
  def increment
    @value += 1
  end
end
first = Counter.new
second = Counter.new(10)
first.increment
first.increment
first.increment
p first.value
p second.value
experiments.answer: This run increments first three times, so its value is 3; Example increments it once, so it is 1. second is a separate object and remains 10 in both runs.

experiments.title: Keep state per object
experiments.task: Create another Lamp with "red" and print its color.
experiments.answer: Each new instance receives its own @color value, so the second lamp reports red.

experiments.title: Update instance state
experiments.task: Call increment two more times before printing. What is value?
experiments.code:
class Counter
  def initialize
    @value = 0
  end
  def increment
    @value += 1
  end
  def value
    @value
  end
end
counter = Counter.new
counter.increment
p counter.value
experiments.answer: Each call adds one to this counter object, so value becomes 3.

title: Share behavior with modules
goal: Include instance behavior and organize names with a module.
paragraphs: A module can group related names and define methods for reuse. include makes a module’s instance methods available to instances of the including class. You cannot instantiate a module with new.
Modules also provide namespaces. Qualify a nested constant with :: to identify where it belongs. include, extend and prepend serve different purposes; this lesson demonstrates include only.
code:
module Named
  def label
    "item: #{name}"
  end
end
class Product
  include Named
  def name
    "book"
  end
end
puts Product.new.label
pitfall: Included methods can depend on methods of their receiver. Those dependencies still need to be implemented by the class.
remaining: extend, prepend, method lookup order and namespace resolution need dedicated examples.

experiments.title: Compare the included method
experiments.task: Compare this output with Example: which part changes when Product#name returns pen?
experiments.code:
module Named
  def label
    "item: #{name}"
  end
end
class Product
  include Named
  def name
    "pen"
  end
end
puts Product.new.label
experiments.answer: The label changes from item: book to item: pen. The included label method calls name on the Product instance.

experiments.title: Include a method
experiments.task: Change greet to return "Welcome". What prints?
experiments.code:
module Greeter
  def greet
    "Hello"
  end
end
class Person
  include Greeter
end
puts Person.new.greet
experiments.answer: The included instance method is available to Person instances, and now returns Welcome.

experiments.title: Call an included method
experiments.task: Change Book#kind to return "novel". What does description print?
experiments.code:
module Describable
  def description
    "A #{kind}"
  end
end
class Book
  include Describable
  def kind
    "book"
  end
end
puts Book.new.description
experiments.answer: The included method calls kind on the same Book object, producing A novel.

title: Handle an expected failure
goal: Raise an exception, handle a specific error and run cleanup.
paragraphs: An exception interrupts normal execution. rescue handles a matching exception so your program can respond. Prefer a specific exception class when you know which failure you can recover from.

ensure runs when leaving its protected block during normal Ruby control flow, including exception propagation. It is useful for cleanup. Browser termination or stopping the Worker is outside this guarantee.
code:
begin
  Integer("not a number")
rescue ArgumentError
  puts "Please use digits"
ensure
  puts "Attempt finished"
end
begin
  raise ArgumentError, "score must be positive"
rescue ArgumentError => error
  puts error.message
end
output:
Please use digits
Attempt finished
score must be positive
pitfall: A broad rescue can hide programming errors. Handling a failure should have a specific purpose.
remaining: Custom exception classes, else, retry and exception cause chains are not covered yet.

experiments.title: Compare handled and successful conversion
experiments.task: Compare this run with Example: which message disappears, and why does Attempt finished remain?
experiments.code:
begin
  Integer("42")
rescue ArgumentError
  puts "Please use digits"
ensure
  puts "Attempt finished"
end
begin
  raise ArgumentError, "score must be positive"
rescue ArgumentError => error
  puts error.message
end
experiments.output:
Attempt finished
score must be positive
experiments.answer: Please use digits disappears because converting 42 succeeds, so rescue does not run. ensure still prints Attempt finished as the protected block ends.

experiments.title: Rescue a specific error
experiments.task: Replace "oops" with "12". Does the rescue run?
experiments.code:
begin
  Integer("oops")
rescue ArgumentError
  puts "invalid number"
end
experiments.answer: Conversion succeeds for 12, so no ArgumentError is raised and nothing prints.

experiments.title: Always run ensure
experiments.task: Raise an ArgumentError inside begin. Does ensure still print done?
experiments.code:
begin
  puts "working"
ensure
  puts "done"
end
experiments.answer: ensure runs as Ruby leaves the protected block, including while an exception propagates.

title: Match structured data
goal: Select a branch using the shape and values of a Hash.
paragraphs: Pattern matching examines a value’s structure. In a case/in expression, a hash pattern can require particular keys and bind values to local variables. This is useful when handling data with several possible shapes.
The role value below must equal "admin". The name: shorthand binds the associated value to name. The else branch handles a mismatch; without a matching branch or else, case/in raises an error.
code:
user = { name: "Ruby", role: "admin" }
case user
in { name:, role: "admin" }
  puts "Welcome, #{name}"
else
  puts "Guest"
end
pitfall: A hash pattern can allow extra keys. Use an explicit restrictive pattern when extra keys must be rejected.
remaining: Array/find patterns, pins, guards, deconstruction and rightward assignment are not covered yet.

experiments.title: Compare matching roles
experiments.task: Compare this output with Example: why does this data select Guest?
experiments.code:
user = { name: "Ruby", role: "member" }
case user
in { name:, role: "admin" }
  puts "Welcome, #{name}"
else
  puts "Guest"
end
experiments.answer: The role is member here, so the pattern requiring admin does not match and the else branch prints Guest. Example has role admin and prints Welcome, Ruby.

experiments.title: Match a hash shape
experiments.task: Change count to 5. Which bound value changes?
experiments.answer: The hash pattern binds count from the matching key, so the printed count becomes 5.

experiments.title: Choose a matching branch
experiments.task: Change code to 200. Which branch matches?
experiments.answer: The first hash pattern requires code: 200, so it prints ok.

title: Scope a method extension with refinements
goal: Activate an extension in a lexical scope.
paragraphs: Reopening a class changes methods for its users broadly. A refinement can limit where an extension is active. Define the extension inside refine, then activate the containing module with using.

Activation follows where code is defined, not simply which object is passed around. A method defined outside the active scope does not gain the refinement merely because a caller activated it. Keep this distinction in mind when splitting code into methods.
code:
module ExcitedText
  refine String do
    def excited
      self + "!"
    end
  end
end
using ExcitedText
puts "Ruby".excited
pitfall: using cannot be activated inside a method. Refinements are not a general global extension mechanism.
remaining: Refinement method lookup and interactions with inheritance and imports are not covered yet.

experiments.title: Compare refined behavior
experiments.task: Compare this output with Example: what changes when the refined method uses upcase?
experiments.code:
module ExcitedText
  refine String do
    def excited
      upcase + "!"
    end
  end
end
using ExcitedText
puts "Ruby".excited
experiments.answer: The output changes from Ruby! to RUBY! because upcase converts the receiver to uppercase before appending !.

experiments.title: Activate a refinement
experiments.task: Change the string to "Blocks". What does short return?
experiments.code:
module ShortNames
  refine String do
    def short
      self[0, 3]
    end
  end
end
using ShortNames
puts "Ruby language".short
experiments.answer: The refined method slices the first three characters, so it returns Blo.

experiments.title: Limit the refined call
experiments.task: Change the receiver to "Ruby". What is wrapped?
experiments.code:
module Bracketed
  refine String do
    def bracket
      "[#{self}]"
    end
  end
end
using Bracketed
puts "code".bracket
experiments.answer: The method is active after using and wraps its receiver, producing [Ruby].

title: Recognize alias, undef, BEGIN and END
goal: Identify less common forms and their effect on execution.
paragraphs: alias introduces another name for an existing method at that point in the program. undef makes a method unavailable through that class. These forms affect an interface, so ordinary method definitions are often clearer when no aliasing is needed.

BEGIN executes before the main body and END registers work for normal Ruby process exit. In this playground, the host evaluates the code and then terminates its Worker without a normal Ruby process shutdown. The END block below therefore does not print finish here; running the same program with a local ruby command does print it. The expected output documents the browser behavior.
code:
BEGIN { puts "start" }
class Message
  def text
    "hello"
  end
  alias original_text text
  undef text
end
puts Message.new.original_text
p Message.new.respond_to?(:text)
END { puts "finish" }
pitfall: Do not use END for cleanup in this playground. Its execution lifecycle differs from running a Ruby script as a command-line process.
remaining: Multiple END blocks and alias behavior across later method redefinitions need further examples.

experiments.title: Compare method availability
experiments.task: Compare respond_to? here with Example: what changed when undef was removed?
experiments.code:
BEGIN { puts "start" }
class Message
  def text
    "hello"
  end
  alias original_text text
end
puts Message.new.original_text
p Message.new.respond_to?(:text)
END { puts "finish" }
experiments.answer: respond_to?(:text) changes from false to true. Without undef, the class still exposes text as well as its alias original_text.

experiments.title: Alias a method
experiments.task: Change text to return "welcome" and run again. What does the alias call?
experiments.code:
class Greeting
  def text
    "hello"
  end
  alias message text
end
puts Greeting.new.message
experiments.answer: Editing the definition before alias changes the body that message refers to, so it prints welcome. The alias is created after that definition when you run the code.

experiments.title: Check method availability
experiments.task: Remove undef text. What does respond_to? return?
experiments.code:
class Greeting
  def text
    "hello"
  end
  undef text
end
p Greeting.new.respond_to?(:text)
experiments.answer: The method is available again, so respond_to? returns true.

title: Code layout and line breaks
goal: Separate Ruby expressions clearly and continue an expression across lines.
paragraphs: Ruby treats a line break as the end of an expression when the expression is complete. A semicolon can separate expressions on one line, though separate lines are usually easier to read. Indentation helps people see structure; it does not replace Ruby's syntax.

Ruby can continue an expression when the current line is incomplete, such as after +. In that case the next line belongs to the same expression. Use parentheses or a clear line break to show how the parts fit together.
code:
first = 2
second = 3
total = first +
  second
puts total

experiments.title: Separate statements
experiments.task: Predict the two printed lines. Then put the assignments on separate lines without changing their values.
experiments.code:
first = 2; second = 3
puts first
puts second
experiments.answer: The semicolon separates the two assignments, so Ruby prints 2 and then 3. Moving each assignment to its own line keeps the same output and is easier to scan.

experiments.title: Continue an expression
experiments.task: What does total contain? Change the second addend from 3 to 8 and predict the new output.
experiments.code:
total = 10 +
  3
puts total
experiments.answer: The plus sign leaves the expression incomplete, so the next line supplies its right-hand value. Changing 3 to 8 makes the output 18.

experiments.title: Use parentheses
experiments.task: This expression continues inside parentheses. Predict the result, then change 4 to 6. Does putting the grouped sum on separate lines change the calculation?
experiments.code:
total = (
  2 + 4
) * 3
puts total
experiments.answer: The open parenthesis lets the grouped expression continue across lines. The result is 18; changing 4 to 6 makes it 24. Line breaks inside this grouping do not change the arithmetic.

pitfall: A line break after a complete expression starts a new expression. Put a continuation operator such as + at the end of the unfinished line, or use parentheses to make the grouping clear.
remaining: Backslash line continuation and optional separators in control structures are not covered.

title: Comments
goal: Add notes to Ruby code with comments that Ruby does not execute.
paragraphs: A comment begins with # and continues to the end of that line. You can put it on its own line or after Ruby code. Ruby ignores the comment text, so it does not change the program's output.
Use comments to explain a reason or intention that the code does not make clear. Keep executable Ruby outside the comment so the interpreter can run it.
code:
# Choose a value for the greeting
name = "Ruby" # this is a short comment
puts "Hello, #{name}!"

experiments.title: Comment out a line
experiments.task: Predict the output. Then remove the # before the first puts and predict both lines.
experiments.code:
# puts "First line"
puts "Second line"
experiments.answer: Ruby ignores the first line because it starts with #. Removing that # makes the first puts run too, so both lines print.

experiments.title: Add an end-of-line note
experiments.task: What prints before the #? Change the number to 9 and predict the result.
experiments.code:
count = 4 # number of tries
puts count
experiments.answer: The text after # is a comment, so puts prints the assigned value 4. Changing the number to 9 makes it print 9.

experiments.title: Keep code outside the comment
experiments.task: Predict the output, then change "Ready" to "Done". Which text is part of the comment?
experiments.code: puts "Ready" # show the status
experiments.answer: Ruby runs puts and ignores the note after #. Changing the string changes the output to Done; the words after # still have no effect.

pitfall: Text after # on a line is a comment, including anything that looks like Ruby code. Put the code before # or on a separate line if it should run.
remaining: Block comments and magic comments are not covered.

title: Operators are methods
goal: Read common operators as methods called on the value to their left.
paragraphs: Many Ruby operators are methods. The expression 2 + 3 can also be written as 2.+(3): the value on the left is the receiver, and the value on the right is passed to its + method.

The same operator can do different work for different receiver types. Integer + adds numbers, while String + joins text. This lesson uses built-in objects; defining operators for a custom class is a separate topic.

experiments.title: Compare two spellings
experiments.task: Predict both results. Change the argument in the method-call form from 3 to 8; what changes?
experiments.answer: Both forms call + on the Integer 2 with 3, so both print 5. Changing the argument to 8 makes the second result 10.

experiments.title: Use plus with strings
experiments.task: What does + do when its receiver is a String? Change the second string to " rules" and predict the output.
experiments.code: p "Ruby" + "!"
experiments.answer: Here + is called on the String "Ruby" and joins the supplied string to it. With " rules", p displays "Ruby rules".

experiments.title: Repeat a string
experiments.task: Predict the output, then change the receiver from "ha" to "go". Which value receives *?
experiments.code: p "ha" * 3
experiments.answer: The String "ha" is the receiver of * and 3 is its argument, so the string repeats three times. With "go", p displays "gogogo".

pitfall: An operator does not have one universal meaning: its receiver determines which method runs. For example, String + joins strings, while Integer + adds numbers.
remaining: Custom operator definitions, precedence and logical operators are outside this lesson.
